Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 104, English)
A Guided Group Astral Journey to Rama Pir's Lok, and the True Purpose of Astral Travel

This session is a guided, live gr oup astral-travel ("lok darshan") exer cise, in which the speaker leads devotees thr ough br eathing and prayer into a shar ed visualization journey towar d the r ealm (lok) of Rama Pir (also called Ramdev Pir / Rama Sarkar), with many devotees narrating their r eal-time impr essions as the journey unfolds. The session closes with an extended teaching on what astral travel is actually for — r eceiving r est, knowledge, and cr eative insight far mor e efficiently than thr ough the physical body alone.
Part A — Preparing for the Journey

1. Opening instructions: The speaker asks all devotees to wash their hands and feet before sitting, remain untouched by others during the exercise, and begin with ten long, deep breaths before opening their eyes and bowing to Dharti Mata (Mother Earth).

2. The congr egational sankalp prayer: The speaker leads a prayer to Hanuman ji Maharaj, of fering the group's jaap, tap, and sadhna as witnessed by the speaker , requesting inclusion in the guru's sankalp, protection, and permission for lok darshan (vision of the realm), followed by "Jai Siyaram" chanting.

3. Guidance on bhav-drishti (intuitive/felt vision): The speaker instructs devotees to look with bhav-drishti — described as often appearing first in black-and-white, or as a felt impression rather than a complete image — and warns that rejecting or second-guessing the first faint impression ("this isn't clear , this is wrong") causes it, and successive images, to be withdrawn; devotees are told to accept and build on whatever comes rather than filtering it through logical doubt.

4. On mixing logic with vision: Per this teaching, trying to reason or ar gue with what one sees, rather than simply observing with feeling, actively interferes with the process — "the one way to connect with the astral world is to surrender ."

5. A second sankalp specifically for this journey: After initial impressions begin, the speaker leads a further specific prayer requesting Hanuman ji Maharaj's permission to be taken to Rama Dev Pir's lok, followed by a direct prayer to Rama Sarkar for the same permission and grace.
Part B — The Shar ed Journey: Recurring Elements Devotees Reported

1. Overview: As the guided journey unfolds, devotees narrate their impressions aloud in real time, and the speaker periodically confirms whether a given impression is "correct" for this stage of the journey . Because so many devotees shared similar or overlapping impressions, the recurring pattern is summarized below rather than attributed name-by-name.

2. Initial white light: The overwhelming majority of devotees first reported an intense, pervasive white light — some described it as blinding or all-encompassing, filling their entire field of vision before any specific shapes emer ged. The speaker confirmed this as correct, explaining that Rama Pir's lok is specifically associated with the tattva of Lord Rama's final avatar , so pure white/bright light at this stage indicated the group was on the right track.

3. A path thr ough clouds or mountains: Several devotees described a path opening through cloud formations or between two mountains, with everything on either side appearing white, sometimes leading toward snow-capped peaks (some specifically likened this to Kailash Mansarovar).

4. A chariot (rath): Many devotees independently described seeing a lar ge, ornate chariot — variously gold, glass, or crystal in appearance, with a canopy (chhatra) overhead, sometimes drawn by white horses — understood as the vehicle gathering and carrying devotees' subtle bodies toward the destination.

5. Guides and escorts (doot): Devotees reported being accompanied or scanned by escort figures (doot) dressed in white, some on horseback, some with lar ge mustaches, spears, or lanterns, described in some accounts as resembling Rajput warriors; devotees were told these figures are the lok's own attendants/gatekeepers.

6. A gr eat white gate: Nearly all devotees eventually described arriving at a very lar ge, ornate white or gold gate, often carved with floral or lotus motifs, sometimes with a second gate visible behind the first, with light streaming from inside before it opened; the speaker confirmed this as the entrance to Rama Pir's lok.

7. Scanning and entry: Several devotees described being scanned by an instrument-like object in the attendants' hands before being allowed through the gate, followed by receiving a small token or gift (coins, wheat, or similar) from local residents as they entered — described by the speaker as ensuring "no one leaves empty-handed."

8. A grand darbar (royal court): Beyond the gate, devotees described an enormous hall or court (darbar), with a lar ge throne at the center , courtiers and saints seated to either side (some appearing as pure light/ener gy due to their intensity), and a red carpet bordered in blue leading toward the throne.

9. Domes, minar ets, and mixed ar chitecture: Several devotees noted the surrounding structures had a Islamicate architectural style (domes, minarets) alongside Hindu temple elements, and the speaker confirmed this reflects the lok's mixed HinduMuslim devotional character (explained further in Part C).

10. A blessing and prasad: Many devotees reported receiving a blessing directly on the head from saints or from Rama Pir himself, and several specifically reported receiving jalebi (a sweet) as prasad.

1 1. Darshan of Rama Pir himself: As the journey progressed, an increasing number of devotees reported the light before the throne resolving into a clear figure — described consistently across many accounts as a regal, mustached man in royal Rajasthani-style dress, wearing a red or maroon turban set with jewels, an ornate long coat (angarkha), a garland, and traditional curled-toe shoes, radiating an intense light from his face and crown that some devotees initially found too bright to look at directly .

12. Other devotees additionally saw Lord Shiva or Lord Vishnu: A number of devotees, on requesting further darshan, separately reported seeing Lord Shiva or a blue, four -armed form of Lord Vishnu; the speaker confirmed both as valid, explaining Rama Pir is regarded, within this lineage's teaching, as an avatar of Rama/V ishnu, so either association is considered correct.
Part C — Who Is Rama Pir?

1. Rama Pir's identity , per this teaching: The speaker explains that Rama Pir (Ramdev Pir/Rama Sarkar) is regarded, within this tradition, as a direct avatar of Lord Rama, and is revered as the "Pir of Pirs" — worshipped by both Hindu and Muslim communities across India and Pakistan.

2. The five-pirs legend: Per this teaching, five pirs once travelled from Mecca specifically to test Ramdev Pir's authenticity; he demonstrated an immediate miracle, and all five bowed to him, acknowledging him as greater than themselves — which the
speaker of fers as the origin of his being called "Pir of Pirs," worshipped across both religious traditions to this day , including in parts of present-day Pakistan.

3. Architecture and inhabitants of the lok: Per this teaching, because of this dual Hindu-Muslim reverence, the lok itself contains a visible mix of architectural and devotional styles — marble domes and minarets alongside Hindu temple motifs — and devotees may encounter figures from both traditions (Sufi saints/pirs as well as Hindu sants) serving there.
Part D — Recognizing a Genuine Blessing

1. The sign of true darshan — stillness, not spectacle: Per this teaching, the clearest sign that a devotee has genuinely received Rama Pir's blessing is not necessarily a vivid or detailed visual, but a specific inner state: a sudden ur ge to stop moving, stop speaking, and simply be still, accompanied by lightness, a sense of complete contentment, and eyes that feel naturally drawn to close.

2. What to do when this stillness occurs: Per this teaching, if a devotee experiences this state, they should bow to Dharti Mata, gently rub their palms together , and touch them to their own eyes as a closing gesture — but if this specific stillness has not occurred, they should remain in the exercise rather than concluding early .

3. Devotees without a clear visual should not feel they missed out: Per this teaching, devotees who saw little or nothing visually were reassured that blessing is never withheld entirely — everyone present, without exception, is said to receive something, even if it manifests only as an unexplained shift in mood, ener gy , or later insight rather than a specific image.
Part E — Why Astral Travel Matters: The 8-Hours-in-40-Minutes Teaching

1. The cor e claim: Per this teaching, astral travel is not merely a devotional curiosity — a person who learns to do it ef fectively can obtain the restorative benefit of roughly eight hours of physical sleep in as little as thirty to forty minutes of meditative astral travel.

2. Why this works — a r elativity framework: Per this teaching, this is explained loosely through an analogy to relativity: the further one's subtle body travels/journeys during astral travel, the more physical-world time is compressed relative to the experience — dif ferent lokas can therefore yield dif ferent subjective "nap" durations.

3. Why saints historically r elied on this technique: Per this teaching, this is why historical saints and mahatmas were said to be able to accomplish so much despite spending long hours in meditation — the meditation session itself functioned as rest, allowing them to return refreshed and continue their work without needing additional physical sleep.

4. Beyond r est — remedies and knowledge fr om other realms: Per this teaching, advanced practitioners historically also used astral travel to retrieve remedies not available in this physical realm (illustrated as a "cure" obtained from another loka, brought back and infused into water via mantra, then given to a physically ill person for healing) — explaining folk accounts of a saint's "blown breath" curing illness as actually describing knowledge/vidya retrieved through this kind of astral travel rather than a simple physical gesture.

5. Three benefits of the technique, summarized: Per this teaching, ef fective astral travel of fers three benefits: (1) rest/ener gy far more ef ficiently than ordinary sleep, (2) the ability to "cure" or resolve problems by drawing knowledge or tattva from elsewhere, and (3) direct transmission of knowledge or ideas from advanced beings encountered in other realms.

6. Creativity as evidence of r eceived knowledge: Per this teaching, highly creative individuals (architects, scientists, artists) are described as unconsciously receiving ideas from exactly this kind of subtle-world source rather than generating them entirely
on their own — with the definition of "artist," per this teaching, extended to anyone who performs their work in an unusually distinctive or excellent way .

7. Sudden insight as a sign of subtle transmission: Per this teaching, the common experience of waking up with a solution to a problem one couldn't solve the night before is of fered as everyday evidence of this same subtle-world knowledge transmission occurring outside conscious awareness.

8. The two things the subtle world actually offers: Per this teaching, contrary to a common assumption that the subtle world is primarily about "ener gy ," the speaker states its two real currencies are knowledge (gyaan) and time (samay) — power/shakti, per this teaching, follows automatically once those two are present, rather than being sought directly .

9. Reassurance for devotees who felt nothing: Per this teaching, even devotees who report seeing "pure black, nothing at all" are promised to have still received something from this exercise — the ef fects, per this teaching, may surface later as a spontaneous idea, a shift in how one speaks or carries oneself, or newfound ease with a previously dif ficult task, rather than as anything noticed in the moment.
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

In guided lok-darshan/astral-travel exercises, accept the first faint bhav-drishti impression rather than rejecting it as unclear — rejecting early impressions causes subsequent ones to stop coming; surrender , not logical analysis, is the way to connect with the astral world. Recurring, broadly-confirmed motifs of this journey to Rama Pir's lok: intense white light, a path through clouds/mountains, an ornate chariot, escort figures (doot), a great white/gold gate, a grand darbar with a central throne, and a blessing/prasad (often jalebi). Rama Pir (Ramdev Pir/Rama Sarkar) is regarded in this teaching as a direct avatar of Lord Rama, revered by both Hindu and Muslim traditions as "Pir of Pirs" — his lok reflects this mixed architectural and devotional character . The clearest sign of a genuine blessing received in this exercise is not necessarily a vivid image but an inner stillness — a natural ur ge to stop moving, speaking, or seeking more, paired with contentment and closing eyes. No devotee present is left without some form of blessing, even those who saw nothing visually; benefits may surface later rather than in the moment. Effective astral travel can provide the restorative benefit of roughly eight hours of sleep in about 30–40 minutes, historically used by saints to rest ef ficiently while devoting long hours to practice. Beyond rest, astral travel is described as a means of retrieving remedies/knowledge (vidya) from other realms and receiving direct creative/intellectual insight — the two real "currencies" of the subtle world, per this teaching, are knowledge and time, with power/shakti following automatically .

Bot Response Guidelines

Present the guided journey's recurring visual motifs (white light, chariot, gate, darbar , Rama Pir's described appearance) as this specific group session's collective, real-time experience, not as a fixed or universally guaranteed itinerary for every future practitioner . Present the astral-travel ef ficiency claims (8 hours of rest in 30–40 minutes, remedies retrieved from other realms) as this teaching's own devotional framework, not as medically or scientifically verified claims. Reassure users who ask about seeing "nothing" during meditation/visualization practice with this session's explicit teaching (Q17, Q25) that this does not mean no benefit was received. Because most devotees in this session's live narration were not individually named in the source material, do not invent names or identifying details when referencing specific accounts. Spelling note: the institute's name is written "Ashaeiynn" — use this spelling consistently .
Part III — Curated Conversational Q&A (Hinglish)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Curated Conversational Q&A (Session 104, Hinglish)
A Guided Group Astral Journey to Rama Pir's Lok, and the True Purpose of Astral Travel

This is NOT an exhaustive transcript of every exchange in this session. Given that most of this session is a shar ed, r eal-time gr oup narration of a guided journey (documented in full in Part I), only a few standalone exchanges of lasting, general value ar e curated her e, each with a short italicized rationale note.
Exchange 1 — "Let x = a": Trusting the First Impr ession

Bhaiya: Bhav drishti mein sabko dikhega. Dimaag jo lagayega usko kuch nahi dikhega. Kabhi-kabhi toh sir bharose pe chalna padta hai — aur starting mein hum maan lete hain "let x = a." Toh usi prakar se ek baar aapko bhav drishti se dekhna shuru karna hai. Jo log yeh kehte hain "mujhe dikhayi nahi deta," sir aap bhav drishti se nahi dekhte. Bhaiya (continuing): Jab aap pehli mein hi mana kar dete ho "nahi yeh saaf nahi hai, yeh galat hai," toh aap pehli image ko reject kar rahe ho. Fir doosri ko kar diya, teesri ko kar diya... fir devdoot hat jaate hain, dikhana band kar dete hain.

Why this is her e: A concise, quotable teaching moment on how to appr oach any meditative/visualization practice — trust the first faint impr ession rather than logically filtering it out — likely useful well beyond this one session.
Exchange 2 — Why This Matters: Rest, Not Just Ritual

Bhaiya: Agar tumhe yeh tatva samajh aa jaata hai toh aaj raat ko tumhe neend nahi aayegi. Kyunki 8 ghante ki urja ko 40 minute mein prapt karne ki sabse jabardast technique hai yeh. Isiliye dev ताओं ke darshan kiye jaate the, sant mahatma aaj bhi is urja ka istemal karte hain. Astral travel sirf ek khilona nahi hai. Devotee: (implicit, via the session's framing) Toh hum astral travel kyu karte hain? Bhaiya: Kyunki wahan jaakar tum so aao. 40 minute wahan ke 8 ghante yahan ke barabar hote hain. Isiko bolte hain time travel.

Why this is her e: Directly answers the practical "why bother with astral travel" question in the speaker's own wor ds, and is likely to be asked by anyone encountering this practice for the first time.
Note on Curation

This session's content is overwhelmingly a shared, real-time group narration of a single guided journey , with dozens of devotees each briefly describing what they saw as it unfolded — this is summarized as a set of recurring, cross-confirmed motifs in Part I rather than reproduced turn-by-turn here, since most individual devotees were not clearly named in the source material and the exchanges themselves are lar gely repetitive descriptions rather than distinct question-and-answer content. The two exchanges above were chosen because they capture standalone, reusable teaching points rather than one-time visual descriptions.
